title: "I see no good in killing my kin" (1.28–1.39)
hook: his legs give way, his mouth goes dry, the bow slips, and the greatest warrior alive makes his case against the war

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna asked to see, and Achyuta, the unfailing one, stopped the chariot before his grandfather and teacher. Your line was look at them. Today, what Arjuna says when he's done looking.

Think about the last time your body knew before you did. A phone call you didn't want to make, and your hands went cold. A room you didn't want to walk into, and your stomach turned. Arjuna has just looked at his whole family lined up to fight him, and before he can make a single argument, his body makes it for him. His legs give way. His mouth dries up. He's shaking. The hair on his arms stands up. His skin burns. Gandiva, the famous bow, starts slipping from his hand. He can't stand. Then the words come.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS FIRST.` → `LEGS GIVE WAY, MOUTH GOES DRY.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Chapter one, verses twenty-eight to thirty-nine, is Arjuna's objection, worth hearing on its own terms, because the Gita takes it seriously. Is it cowardice? Many readers hear conscience. The heart of it, in Sanskrit: na cha shreyo 'nupashyami hatva svajanam ahave. I see no good in killing my own people in battle. Then further: na kankshe vijayam Krishna, na cha rajyam sukhani cha. I don't want victory, Krishna, or a kingdom, or pleasures. What would a kingdom be for, he asks, if the people we wanted it for are lying dead on this field? Teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles. Even if they kill me, he says, I don't want to kill them, not for all three worlds, let alone this earth. Then his sharpest point. Yes, the Kauravas are in the wrong; greed clouds their minds, and they can't see the evil of destroying a family. But we can, he says. Why shouldn't we, who see clearly, turn back? That's a real argument. People have made it at every war since. And the Gita gives Arjuna twelve verses to make his case, fully, in his own words, before anyone answers. Krishna doesn't interrupt. When he answers, in the next chapter, his first words are blunt: he calls this a weakness of the heart. Commentators have argued ever since over whether it's conscience or confusion. But the reply, which takes the rest of the book, answers this: the honest objection, heard in full. A good teacher lets you say the whole thing.
screen: `COWARDICE, OR CONSCIENCE?` · `I SEE NO GOOD IN KILLING MY KIN.` · `NO KINGDOM IS WORTH THEM.` · `THEY CAN'T SEE. WE CAN. TURN BACK.` · then, large: `HEARD IN FULL.`

segments.voice: Think of something in front of you that part of you really doesn't want to do, and first notice where your body tightens or goes cold. Then let the objection talk, fully, in its own words, the way Arjuna's does. Don't answer, argue or shame it; just listen to the end.
Gandiva, Arjuna's famous bow, slipping from his hand as his legs give way. Arjuna's case against the war: no victory, no kingdom, is worth the people he loves.
Your line: the honest objection. Krishna's answer starts in chapter two. Day one hundred fifty-nine, in the books.

howItsDone: Commentators on the Gita treat Arjuna's objection in 1.28–1.39 as a serious moral argument, and many readers see in it their own moments of doubt before a hard duty; the rest of the Gita is Krishna's answer to it.

notes: Physical symptoms, 1.28–1.30 (limbs fail, mouth dries, trembling, hair on end, skin burns, Gandiva slips, cannot stand). Confirm.
1.35: 'not even for the three worlds, let alone the earth'. Paraphrased. Confirm.
1.38–39: the Kauravas' minds overcome by greed; 'why should we not turn back?'. Paraphrased. Confirm.
'Not cowardice: conscience' is the script's framing; some traditional commentators (e.g. Shankara) read Arjuna's state as delusion born of attachment. A Keeper may want both readings named.
Verse count: 1.28–1.39 is twelve verses. Confirm (numbering varies slightly between editions).
Trapdoor: shreyas returns at 2.7 and 3.2. Confirm.
